title: Composition, context, forms, performance
blurb: Context, compound components, forms, optimistic updates, accessibility and routing — the parts of React you get asked about once past the basics.

questions.q: What problem does Context solve, and what does it cost?
choices: It avoids prop drilling, but every consumer re-renders whenever the value changes
It replaces Redux entirely with no downsides
It makes state global and persistent
questions.why: Context is dependency injection, not a state manager. If a fast-changing value shares a provider with a slow-changing one, everything re-renders — split the contexts, or memoise the value object.
questions.asked: 'When would you use context?' The wrong answer is 'instead of Redux, for all state'.

questions.q: Why does this provider re-render every consumer on each parent render?
choices: The object literal is a new reference each render
questions.why: Context compares the value with Object.is. Wrap it: `useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme }), [theme])`. setTheme from useState is already stable.

questions.q: What is prop drilling, and is it always bad?
choices: Passing props through components that don't use them — usually fine at two or three levels
Passing too many props to one component
questions.why: Reaching for context at the first sign of drilling replaces an explicit, greppable data flow with an invisible one. Composition — passing elements as children — often removes the drilling without any context at all.

questions.q: How does passing `children` avoid a re-render?
choices: children is created by the parent, so Slow re-rendering does not recreate that element
children is always memoised by React
It does not — children always re-render
Because Slow is a class component
questions.why: The element object was made in the parent's render. If Slow re-renders for its own reasons, React sees the identical children element and can skip that subtree. It is memoisation without React.memo.
questions.asked: A sophisticated answer to 'how would you optimise this tree?'

questions.q: What are compound components?
choices: A set of components sharing implicit state through context, like `<Tabs><Tab/></Tabs>`
questions.why: The consumer composes markup naturally instead of passing a config array of props. The trade-off is a less explicit API and required context, so it earns its place mainly in design systems.

questions.q: What is an optimistic update?
choices: Applying the change in the UI immediately and rolling back if the request fails
Prefetching data before it is needed
Assuming the server is always available
questions.why: It makes an app feel instant. It requires you to keep the previous state to restore, and to surface the rollback clearly — silently reverting is worse than a spinner.
questions.asked: Common for mid-level frontend roles; the follow-up is 'how do you handle the failure case?'

questions.q: When should form validation run?
choices: On blur and on submit; switch to on-change only after a field has errored once
On every keystroke from the start
questions.why: Validating each keystroke shows 'invalid email' while someone is typing the second character. Validate on blur, then live-validate that field once it has errored so the message clears as they fix it. The server must validate regardless.

questions.q: How do you prevent a double submit?
choices: Disable the button while the request is in flight, tracked in state
Use a ref to count clicks
Rely on the server rejecting duplicates
questions.why: The UI fix is a submitting flag. The robust fix is both: disabled button plus server-side idempotency, because a retry or a double-tap on flaky mobile can still get two requests through.

questions.q: What makes a modal accessible?
choices: Focus moves in and is trapped, Escape closes it, background is inert, and it is labelled with role="dialog"
A high z-index and a dark overlay
questions.why: Also: return focus to the element that opened it. A portal solves the stacking-context problem but does nothing for accessibility — and focus follows the React tree, not the DOM tree.
questions.asked: A strong mid-level signal — most candidates only mention the overlay.

questions.q: What is a portal for?
choices: Rendering into a DOM node outside the parent, while keeping React context and event bubbling
questions.why: It escapes `overflow: hidden` and z-index stacking for modals, tooltips and toasts. Events still bubble through the React tree, which surprises people expecting DOM behaviour.

questions.q: Why put table filters in the URL query string?
choices: The view becomes shareable, bookmarkable and survives a refresh or a back-button press
questions.why: 'Send me that filtered view' is a real user need. It also gives you back/forward for free. The rule of thumb: state that describes *what you are looking at* belongs in the URL.
questions.asked: A design question that shows product sense as well as React knowledge.

questions.q: What does list virtualisation do?
choices: Renders only the rows in view plus a buffer, keeping DOM node count constant
Loads data lazily as you scroll
questions.why: 10,000 rows means 10,000 DOM nodes and a frozen page. Virtualising keeps ~30 mounted. The costs: variable row heights are hard, and Ctrl-F stops finding off-screen content.

questions.q: What is the difference between infinite scroll and pagination, from an engineering view?
choices: Infinite scroll needs cursor-based paging and accumulating state; pagination can use offsets and replaces state
They are the same with different styling
questions.why: Offset paging with a live dataset duplicates or skips rows as items are inserted. Infinite scroll also breaks the footer, breaks back-navigation position, and needs a keyboard-accessible alternative.

questions.q: How do you make a component controlled *and* uncontrolled?
choices: Accept an optional `value` prop; fall back to internal state when it is undefined
Always keep internal state and sync it in an effect
Use a ref for both cases
questions.why: The standard 'controllable' pattern used by every component library. The trap is syncing a prop into state with an effect, which produces two sources of truth and a render of lag.

questions.q: What is the keyboard contract for a dropdown menu?
choices: Arrow keys move between items, Enter selects, Escape closes, Tab leaves the menu
questions.why: Roving tabindex: the menu is one tab stop and arrows move within it. Making every item tabbable is the common mistake — it forces a keyboard user through 40 stops to get past your menu.

questions.q: How do you test a component well?
choices: Assert on what a user sees and does — rendered text, roles, interactions — not on internal state
questions.why: Tests coupled to implementation break on every refactor and pass through real bugs. Querying by role also catches accessibility problems for free.
questions.asked: The Testing Library philosophy question; expect it for any React role that mentions tests.

questions.q: What is wrong with syncing a prop into state?
choices: It only reads the prop on the first render, so later prop changes are ignored
Nothing — this is the standard way to make a default
questions.why: useState's argument is the *initial* value. If you meant 'reset when the prop changes', change the key. If you meant 'defaultValue', name the prop that way so the one-shot behaviour is documented.

questions.q: You are asked to make a slow page faster. What do you do first?
choices: Profile it to find what actually re-renders and how long
questions.why: The React Profiler tells you which component, how often and how long. Optimising by guesswork usually adds complexity and moves nothing — and sometimes makes it slower.
questions.asked: Whether you measure before optimising is one of the clearest seniority signals there is.

questions.q: What is code splitting in a React app?
choices: Loading route or feature bundles on demand with lazy + Suspense instead of one large bundle
questions.why: The usual first cut is per route. Watch for a waterfall — lazy-loading a component that then fetches its own data serialises two round trips.

questions.q: What does a router give you beyond swapping components?
choices: URL as state, back/forward, deep links, and per-route data loading and code splitting
questions.why: Building a hash router by hand makes this concrete: you end up implementing history, param parsing and matching yourself, which is why the answer to 'why use a router' is not 'because everyone does'.

questions.q: When is a global state manager justified over context plus local state?
choices: When many unrelated components read and write overlapping server or session state frequently
As soon as two components share a value
questions.why: Much of what used to go in Redux is server cache, which a data-fetching library handles better. What remains — session, UI shell, cross-cutting toggles — is often small enough for context.
questions.asked: An opinion question. Distinguishing server state from client state is the strong move.

questions.q: What is the risk of `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`?
choices: It injects raw HTML, so unsanitised content is an XSS vulnerability
It breaks the virtual DOM diff
questions.why: React escapes interpolated values by default, which is why XSS is rare in React apps — this prop is the explicit opt-out. Sanitise with something like DOMPurify, and never pass raw user input.

questions.q: How would you implement undo/redo?
choices: Keep past, present and future stacks of immutable states and move entries between them
Store a diff for each change and reverse it
Re-fetch the previous state from the server
Use useRef to store the last value
questions.why: Immutable state makes this almost free — each state is a snapshot you can hold on to. It is also the strongest practical argument for not mutating state.
